variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- The all-ones signless-Laplacian quadratic form of a graph equals four
    times the number of edges: each edge facet contributes `2² = 4`. -/
theorem slQuad_edgeFacet_one (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj] :
    slQuad (edgeFacet G) (fun _ => 1) = 4 * G.edgeFinset.card := by
  unfold slQuad
  have hterm : ∀ f : G.edgeFinset, (∑ r ∈ edgeFacet G f, (1 : ℝ)) ^ 2 = 4 := by
    intro f
    rw [Finset.sum_const, edgeFacet_card_two]
    norm_num
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun f _ => hterm f)]
  rw [Finset.sum_const]
  simp only [Finset.card_univ, Fintype.card_coe, nsmul_eq_mul]
  ring

    signless-Laplacian quadratic form `4m` and squared norm `n`, so its
    Rayleigh quotient `4m/n` lies below the spectral radius. -/
theorem graph_specRad_ge (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (hV : Fintype.card V ≠ 0) :
    (4 * G.edgeFinset.card : ℝ) / Fintype.card V ≤ specRad (edgeFacet G) := by
  have hnorm : (∑ r : V, ((fun _ => (1 : ℝ)) r) ^ 2) = Fintype.card V := by
    simp [Finset.card_univ]
  have hne : (∑ r : V, ((fun _ => (1 : ℝ)) r) ^ 2) ≠ 0 := by
    rw [hnorm]; exact_mod_cast hV
  have hkey := le_specRad (edgeFacet G) (fun _ => 1) hne
  rw [slQuad_edgeFacet_one, hnorm] at hkey
  exact hkey

/-- **The signless-Laplacian sandwich** `4m/n ≤ q(G) ≤ 2Δ`.  The lower bound
    is the all-ones Rayleigh quotient; the upper bound is the Cauchy–Schwarz
    bound of `Core`/`Bridge` with `D` any common degree bound. -/
theorem graph_specRad_sandwich (G : SimpleGraph V) [DecidableRel G.Adj]
    (D : ℕ) (hD : ∀ v, degree (edgeFacet G) v ≤ D) (hV : Fintype.card V ≠ 0) :
    (4 * G.edgeFinset.card : ℝ) / Fintype.card V ≤ specRad (edgeFacet G) ∧
      specRad (edgeFacet G) ≤ (2 * D : ℝ) :=
  ⟨graph_specRad_ge G hV, graph_specRad_le G D hD⟩

end SignlessLaplacian

open SimpleGraph Finset

namespace SignlessLaplacian

variable {V : Type*} [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V]

/-- `G` contains `t` pairwise vertex-disjoint triangles (`tK_3 ⊆ G`): a family
    `T : Fin t → Finset V` of `3`-cliques that are pairwise disjoint. -/
def HasTDisjTriangles (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ) : Prop :=
  ∃ T : Fin t → Finset V,
    (∀ i, G.IsNClique 3 (T i)) ∧ (∀ i j, i ≠ j → Disjoint (T i) (T j))

/-- `G` is `tK_3`-free: it does not contain `t` pairwise vertex-disjoint
    triangles. -/
def TK3Free (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ) : Prop := ¬ HasTDisjTriangles G t

/-- **The order threshold.**  If `G` contains `t` pairwise-disjoint triangles
    then it has at least `3t` vertices: the triangles' disjoint union has
    exactly `3t` elements. -/
theorem card_ge_of_hasTDisjTriangles (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ)
    (h : HasTDisjTriangles G t) : 3 * t ≤ Fintype.card V := by
  obtain ⟨T, hclique, hdisj⟩ := h
  have hpd : ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin t)) : Set (Fin t)).PairwiseDisjoint T := by
    intro i _ j _ hij
    exact hdisj i j hij
  have hunion : (Finset.univ.biUnion T).card = 3 * t := by
    rw [Finset.card_biUnion hpd]
    rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (fun i _ => (hclique i).card_eq)]
    simp [mul_comm]

    _ ≤ Fintype.card V := Finset.card_le_univ _

    `tK_3`-free: there is simply no room for `t` disjoint triangles.  This is
    why `3t` is the natural conjectural threshold. -/
theorem tK3Free_of_card_lt (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ)
    (h : Fintype.card V < 3 * t) : TK3Free G t := by
  intro hcontra
  exact absurd (card_ge_of_hasTDisjTriangles G t hcontra) (not_le.mpr h)

/-- Containing `tK_3` is monotone in the subgraph order: adding edges can only
    create more triangles. -/
theorem hasTDisjTriangles_mono {G G' : SimpleGraph V} (h : G ≤ G') {t : ℕ}

  obtain ⟨T, hclique, hdisj⟩ := ht
  exact ⟨T, fun i => (hclique i).mono h, hdisj⟩

omit [Fintype V] [DecidableEq V] in
/-- `tK_3`-freeness is antitone in the subgraph order: a subgraph of a
    `tK_3`-free graph is `tK_3`-free. -/
theorem tK3Free_anti {G G' : SimpleGraph V} (h : G ≤ G') {t : ℕ}
    (hfree : TK3Free G' t) : TK3Free G t := by
  intro ht
  exact hfree (hasTDisjTriangles_mono h ht)

    exact h ⟨fun _ => s, fun _ => hs, fun i j hij => absurd (Subsingleton.elim i j) hij⟩
  · rintro h ⟨T, hclique, _⟩

/-- **The clique-cover bound — why the conjectured extremiser is `tK_3`-free.**
    If a vertex set `C` of size `< t` meets every triangle of `G` (equivalently,
    `G` has no triangle disjoint from `C`), then `G` is `tK_3`-free.  `t`
    disjoint triangles would each have to spend a *distinct* vertex inside `C`,
    but `C` has fewer than `t` vertices.

    This is exactly the mechanism behind the construction `K_{t-1} ∨ H` with `H`

    every triangle of the join meets `C`, and `|C| = t-1 < t`. -/
theorem tK3Free_of_clique_cover (G : SimpleGraph V) (t : ℕ) (C : Finset V)
    (hC : C.card < t) (hcov : ∀ S, G.IsNClique 3 S → (S ∩ C).Nonempty) :
    TK3Free G t := by
  rintro ⟨T, hclique, hdisj⟩
  -- pick, for each triangle `T i`, a vertex of `C` it contains

    intro i
    obtain ⟨v, hv⟩ := hcov (T i) (hclique i)
    rw [Finset.mem_inter] at hv
    exact ⟨v, hv.1, hv.2⟩
  choose f hfT hfC using hmem
  -- `f` is injective: distinct triangles are disjoint, so their chosen vertices differ
  have hinj : Function.Injective f := by
    intro i j hij
    by_contra hne
    have hd : Disjoint (T i) (T j) := hdisj i j hne
    have hi : f i ∈ T i := hfT i
    have hj : f j ∈ T j := hfT j
    rw [hij] at hi
    exact (Finset.disjoint_left.mp hd hi) (hij ▸ hj)
  -- the image of `f` lies in `C`, giving `t ≤ |C| < t`
  have hsub : (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin t)).image f ⊆ C := by
    intro v hv
    obtain ⟨i, _, rfl⟩ := Finset.mem_image.mp hv
    exact hfC i
  have ht_le : t ≤ C.card := by
    calc t = (Finset.univ : Finset (Fin t)).card := by simp
      _ = ((Finset.univ : Finset (Fin t)).image f).card :=
          (Finset.card_image_of_injective _ hinj).symm
      _ ≤ C.card := Finset.card_le_card hsub

# Computational Evidence: `tK_3`-free signless Laplacian extremal problem

This note records the small-case calculations that motivated the formal results in
`TK3Free.lean` and `EdgeLowerBound.lean`.

## 1. The conjectured extremiser and its size

The conjectured extremal graph is `G(n,t) = K_{t-1} ∨ K_{a,b}` with
`a = ⌊(n-t+1)/2⌋`, `b = ⌈(n-t+1)/2⌉`, so `a + b = n - t + 1` and the total order is
`(t-1) + a + b = n`, as required.

Edge count: `m(n,t) = C(t-1,2) + a·b + (t-1)(a+b)`.
The three terms are: the `(t-1)`-clique, the complete bipartite part, and the join edges.

| t | a | b | n=(t-1)+a+b | m   | 2(t-1)+(a+b) |
|---|---|---|-------------|-----|--------------|
| 2 | 3 | 3 | 7           | 15  | 8            |
| 3 | 3 | 3 | 8           | 22  | 10           |
| 4 | 3 | 3 | 9           | 30  | 12           |
| 5 | 3 | 3 | 10          | 39  | 14           |
| 6 | 3 | 3 | 11          | 49  | 16           |
| 7 | 3 | 3 | 12          | 60  | 18           |

(These come from the `#eval` of `edges t a b` used during development.)

## 2. Why the threshold is `3t`, not `28t-17`

`t` vertex-disjoint triangles occupy `3t` distinct vertices. Hence:

* If `n < 3t`, **every** graph on `n` vertices is trivially `tK_3`-free — there is no
  room for `t` disjoint triangles. (Formalised: `tK3Free_of_card_lt`.)
* `n = 3t` is realised with equality by a disjoint union of `t` triangles
  (`card_ge_of_hasTDisjTriangles` is sharp).

So `3t` is the *smallest* order at which "being `tK_3`-free" is a genuine constraint;
this is the structural reason the conjectured threshold is `3t`. The published bound
`28t-17` is an artefact of the proof technique (stability + edge counting), not of the
geometry of the problem.

## 3. The spectral sandwich `4m/n ≤ q(G) ≤ 2Δ`

The signless Laplacian `Q = D + A` satisfies, by the all-ones Rayleigh quotient,
`q(G) ≥ x^T Q x / x^T x = 4m/n` (since `1^T Q 1 = 1^T D 1 + 1^T A 1 = 2m + 2m = 4m`).
The Cauchy–Schwarz / row-sum bound gives `q(G) ≤ 2Δ`. For the conjectured extremiser:

* `Δ(G(n,t)) = n-1` (a clique vertex is adjacent to everyone), so `q ≤ 2(n-1)`.
* `4m/n` grows like `n + 4t + O(1/n)` for fixed `t`, confirming `q` is `Θ(n)` and that
  the dense join is a serious candidate for the maximiser.

Formalised lower bound: `graph_specRad_ge`; sandwich: `graph_specRad_sandwich`.

## 4. Why the construction is `tK_3`-free (clique-cover mechanism)

In `K_{t-1} ∨ H` with `H` triangle-free, every triangle must use at least one of the
`t-1` clique vertices (a triangle entirely inside `H` is impossible). Thus the
`(t-1)`-set `C` of clique vertices is a transversal of all triangles, and `t` disjoint
triangles would need `t` distinct vertices of `C` — impossible since `|C| = t-1`.
Formalised in full generality as `tK3Free_of_clique_cover`.

## 5. Counterexample hunt

No counterexample was sought to the *published* extremal theorem (it is proved for
`n ≥ 28t-17`). The conjecture concerns lowering the threshold; the calculations above
support, rather than refute, the `3t` threshold by showing it is the structurally
forced boundary. The formal results isolate the parts of this picture that hold for
**all** `t` and `n` without any large-`n` hypothesis.

# Future Directions: signless Laplacian spectra of triangle-packing-free graphs

This cycle isolated two robust, threshold-free phenomena underlying the extremal
problem for the signless Laplacian spectral radius of `tK_3`-free graphs: a sharp
order threshold (`3t`) below which the constraint is vacuous, and a two-sided
Rayleigh sandwich `4m/n ≤ q(G) ≤ 2Δ` that controls every candidate graph. The
following conjectures push these findings further.

## 1. The order threshold collapses to `3t` for the spectral extremal problem

**Conjecture.** For every `t ≥ 2` and every `n ≥ 3t`, the unique graph of order `n`
containing no `t` vertex-disjoint triangles that maximises the signless Laplacian
spectral radius is the join of a clique on `t-1` vertices with a balanced complete
bipartite graph on the remaining `n-t+1` vertices.

The key insight is that `3t` is the *combinatorial* boundary at which the
no-`t`-disjoint-triangles condition first becomes a genuine restriction, so any larger
threshold is an artefact of the counting method rather than of the geometry; the
balanced join already saturates the all-ones lower bound `4m/n` while keeping the
maximum degree, hence `2Δ`, as small as a triangle-transversal of size `t-1` allows.

Why now? The published threshold `28t-17` was obtained by stability arguments that
deliberately trade sharpness for uniformity; with the transversal mechanism made exact
(every triangle must spend a vertex on the `(t-1)`-clique), the remaining gap to `3t`
is purely a finite family of small `n`, which is now within reach of direct analysis.

## 2. A degree-corrected lower bound beats `4m/n` for join extremisers

**Conjecture.** For the balanced join extremiser there is a constant `c > 0` such that
`q(G) ≥ (4m/n) + c·(Δ - 2m/n)`, i.e. the spectral radius exceeds the average-degree
proxy by an amount proportional to the degree spread created by the dominating clique.

The key insight is that the all-ones vector is *not* the optimal test vector once a few
vertices (the clique) have far higher degree than average: tilting weight toward the
high-degree clique strictly increases the Rayleigh quotient, and the gain is governed by
the variance of the degree sequence.

Why now? The Rayleigh sandwich just formalised makes the all-ones bound a rigorous
baseline; subtracting it from a tilted-vector bound turns "the clique dominates" from
heuristic into a quantitative, testable inequality.

## 3. The transversal principle characterises all `tK_3`-free extremisers

**Conjecture.** Every signless-Laplacian-extremal `tK_3`-free graph admits a vertex set
of size `t-1` meeting all of its triangles; equivalently, deleting `t-1` vertices makes
the extremiser triangle-free.

The key insight is that maximising spectral radius forces the graph to be as dense as
possible subject to the packing constraint, and the cheapest way to forbid `t` disjoint
triangles while keeping density high is to concentrate all triangles through a tiny
shared transversal — exactly the clique-cover mechanism that makes the conjectured
construction work.

Why now? The clique-cover sufficient condition is now a proved theorem; promoting it to
a *necessary* structural feature of extremisers would convert a construction into a
classification, the natural next milestone.

## 4. The phenomenon is matrix-agnostic across the `A_α` family

**Conjecture.** For the convex family `A_α = αD + (1-α)A` with `α ∈ [0, 1)`, the same
balanced join is the spectral-radius extremiser over `tK_3`-free graphs for all `n ≥ 3t`,
with a single transition value of `α` (if any) where the extremiser changes.

The key insight is that adjacency (`α=0`) and signless Laplacian (`α=1/2`) extremal
results already coincide on the same construction, suggesting the optimum is driven by
the join's global density rather than by the precise diagonal weighting.

Why now? Interpolating matrix families are the current organising principle in spectral
extremal graph theory; the threshold-free sandwich proved here extends verbatim to every
`A_α` with `α < 1`, giving a uniform tool to test the whole family at once.

## 5. Disjoint-`K_r` packings obey an `rt` threshold

**Conjecture.** For fixed `r ≥ 3`, the signless-Laplacian extremiser among graphs with no
`t` vertex-disjoint copies of `K_r` is `K_{t-1}` joined to a balanced complete
`(r-1)`-partite graph, for all `n ≥ rt`.

The key insight is that the counting bound generalises cleanly: `t` disjoint `K_r`'s need
`rt` vertices, and an `(r-1)`-partite part is exactly the densest `K_r`-free fabric on
which to hang the dominating clique, so the `tK_3` story is the `r=3` slice of one family.

Why now? The threshold and clique-cover lemmas formalised here were stated for triangles
but their proofs only use "a copy has `r` vertices" and "a copy disjoint from the
transversal lives in a `K_r`-free part", so the generalisation is immediate to attempt
and would unify several separate papers under one statement.

* `flt_base_lt`     — in a Fermat solution the bases are strictly below `c`.

radical of a perfect-power equation collapses: `rad (aⁿ bⁿ cⁿ)` does not grow with

* `rad_mul_of_coprime` — `rad` is multiplicative on coprime arguments.

with the same set of prime factors; it should be multiplicative on coprime
arguments and totally insensitive to exponents (`rad (n^k) = rad n`).  These two
facts are exactly what lets one replace `rad (a^n b^n c^n)` by `rad (abc)` in the

INSIGHT (Analyst).  `rad (n^k) = rad n` is *purely* a statement about prime-factor

namespace Catalog.NumberTheory.ABC

open Finset

/-- The radical of `n`: the product of the distinct primes dividing `n`. -/
def rad (n : ℕ) : ℕ := ∏ p ∈ n.primeFactors, p

@[simp] lemma rad_zero : rad 0 = 1 := by simp [rad]

@[simp] lemma rad_one : rad 1 = 1 := by simp [rad]

/-- `rad n` divides `n`. -/
lemma rad_dvd (n : ℕ) : rad n ∣ n := Nat.prod_primeFactors_dvd n

/-- `rad n` is always positive (in particular nonzero). -/
lemma rad_pos (n : ℕ) : 0 < rad n := by
  apply Finset.prod_pos
  intro p hp
  exact (Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp).pos

lemma rad_ne_zero (n : ℕ) : rad n ≠ 0 := (rad_pos n).ne'

/-- The radical of a prime is the prime itself. -/
lemma rad_prime {p : ℕ} (hp : p.Prime) : rad p = p := by
  unfold rad
  rw [hp.primeFactors]
  simp

/-- For positive `n`, the radical never exceeds `n`. -/
lemma rad_le_self {n : ℕ} (hn : 0 < n) : rad n ≤ n :=
  Nat.le_of_dvd hn (rad_dvd n)

/-- The radical ignores exponents: `rad (n ^ k) = rad n` for `k ≠ 0`. -/
lemma rad_pow {n k : ℕ} (hk : k ≠ 0) : rad (n ^ k) = rad n := by
  unfold rad
  rw [Nat.primeFactors_pow n hk]

/-
`rad n` is squarefree.
-/
lemma rad_squarefree (n : ℕ) : Squarefree (rad n) := by
  -- The product of distinct primes is squarefree.
  have h_squarefree : ∀ {S : Finset ℕ}, (∀ p ∈ S, Nat.Prime p) → Squarefree (∏ p ∈ S, p) := by
    intros S hS; induction S using Finset.induction <;> simp_all +decide [ Nat.squarefree_mul_iff ] ;
    exact ⟨ Nat.Coprime.prod_right fun p hp => hS.1.coprime_iff_not_dvd.mpr fun h => by have := Nat.prime_dvd_prime_iff_eq hS.1 ( hS.2 p hp ) ; aesop, hS.1.squarefree ⟩;
  exact h_squarefree fun p hp => Nat.prime_of_mem_primeFactors hp

/-
The radical equals `n` exactly when `n` is squarefree (vacuously at `n=0`).
-/
lemma rad_eq_self_iff_squarefree {n : ℕ} :
    rad n = n ↔ Squarefree n := by
  refine ⟨ fun h => ?_, fun h => ?_ ⟩;
  · exact h ▸ rad_squarefree n;
  · convert Nat.prod_primeFactors_of_squarefree h

/-
`rad` is multiplicative on coprime arguments.
-/
lemma rad_mul_of_coprime {m n : ℕ} (h : Nat.Coprime m n) :
    rad (m * n) = rad m * rad n := by
  by_cases hm : m = 0 <;> by_cases hn : n = 0 <;> simp_all +decide [ rad, Nat.primeFactors_mul ];
  rw [ Finset.prod_union ( h.disjoint_primeFactors ) ]

end Catalog.NumberTheory.ABC

We state the **ABC conjecture** using the `rad` framework of `Radical.lean`, and we
prove an *unconditional* fact that motivates the conjecture's shape: there really do
exist coprime triples `a + b = c` with `rad (a b c) < c`.  Hence the naive
inequality `c ≤ rad (a b c)` is **false**, and the `ε`-perturbed exponent
`rad (a b c) ^ (1 + ε)` in the conjecture is genuinely necessary.

## Main definitions / results

* `ABCConjecture` — the statement: for every `ε > 0` there is a constant `K`
  bounding `c` by `K · rad (a b c) ^ (1 + ε)` for all coprime `a + b = c`.
* `exists_abc_triple_rad_lt` — an explicit coprime triple (`1 + 8 = 9`) with
  `rad (a b c) < c`, proved structurally through `rad_mul_of_coprime` and `rad_pow`.

-- !-- Lab Notes -- !--
HYPOTHESIS (Hypothesizer).  Powerful numbers make the radical small relative to the
number itself; combining two powerful coprime summands should beat `rad (abc) ≥ c`.
The smallest case is `1 + 8 = 9`: `rad (1·8·9) = rad 72 = 6 < 9`.

EXPERIMENT (Experimenter).  Rather than `native_decide` on `rad 72`, we compute it
*structurally*: `72 = 2^3 · 3^2`, the factors `8` and `9` are coprime, so
`rad 72 = rad (2^3) · rad (3^2) = 2 · 3 = 6` via `rad_mul_of_coprime`, `rad_pow`,
`rad_prime`.  This is an insight-bearing proof, not a finite check.

CRITIQUE (Critic).  The witness theorem is not vacuous: it exhibits a genuine
triple and the strict inequality `6 < 9`.  It directly shows the `ε = 0`,
`K = 1` form of ABC is false, justifying the conjecture's exponent.
-/

namespace Catalog.NumberTheory.ABC

open scoped Nat

/-- **The ABC conjecture.**  For every `ε > 0` there exists a constant `K > 0` such
that every coprime triple of positive naturals with `a + b = c` satisfies
`c ≤ K · rad (a · b · c) ^ (1 + ε)`. -/
def ABCConjecture : Prop :=
  ∀ ε : ℝ, 0 < ε → ∃ K : ℝ, 0 < K ∧
    ∀ a b c : ℕ, 0 < a → 0 < b → a + b = c → Nat.Coprime a b →
      (c : ℝ) ≤ K * (rad (a * b * c) : ℝ) ^ (1 + ε)

/-- There is a coprime triple `a + b = c` of positive naturals with
`rad (a · b · c) < c`.  Concretely `1 + 8 = 9` with `rad 72 = 6 < 9`.  This shows
the unperturbed inequality `c ≤ rad (a b c)` is false. -/
theorem exists_abc_triple_rad_lt :
    ∃ a b c : ℕ, 0 < a ∧ 0 < b ∧ a + b = c ∧ Nat.Coprime a b ∧
      rad (a * b * c) < c := by
  refine ⟨1, 8, 9, by norm_num, by norm_num, by norm_num, by decide, ?_⟩
  -- `1 * 8 * 9 = 72 = 2^3 * 3^2`, and the two factors are coprime.
  have h72 : (1 * 8 * 9 : ℕ) = 2 ^ 3 * 3 ^ 2 := by norm_num
  have hcop : Nat.Coprime (2 ^ 3) (3 ^ 2) := by decide
  rw [h72, rad_mul_of_coprime hcop, rad_pow (by norm_num : (3 : ℕ) ≠ 0),
      rad_pow (by norm_num : (2 : ℕ) ≠ 0), rad_prime (by norm_num),
      rad_prime (by norm_num)]
  norm_num

end Catalog.NumberTheory.ABC

# Future Directions — Radical, ABC, and its arithmetic shadow

This cycle built a radical-function framework, stated the ABC conjecture over it,
exhibited a genuine high-quality triple, and derived asymptotic Fermat from ABC.
The following conjectures grow directly out of those findings.

## 1. The radical is exponent-blind, so power equations are governed by their bases

**Conjecture.** For every fixed integer `k ≥ 3`, the equation `xᵏ + yᵏ = zᵏ` in
coprime positive integers has no solution once `z` exceeds an absolute, effectively
computable bound that is *independent of `k`*.

The key insight is that the radical of a perfect-power product `xᵏyᵏzᵏ` equals the
radical of `xyz`, so the entire exponential growth of `zᵏ` must be absorbed by a
quantity that does not see the exponent at all — a tension that can only be resolved
by forcing `z` small. Why now? The structural law `rad(nᵏ) = rad n` is exactly the
lever that converts a statement about exponents into a statement about bases, and the
asymptotic-Fermat derivation already isolates this mechanism; sharpening "for large
`k`" to "for all `k ≥ 3` with a `k`-free bound" is the natural next target.

## 2. High-quality triples are powered by repeated squaring

**Conjecture.** There are infinitely many coprime triples `a + b = c` with
`rad(abc) < c / 2ᵐ` for arbitrarily large `m`, realised by the family
`1 + (3^(2ⁿ) − 1) = 3^(2ⁿ)`, whose middle term is divisible by an ever-higher power
of two.

The key insight is that `3^(2ⁿ) − 1` accumulates one extra factor of two with each
squaring (a lifting-the-exponent phenomenon), so the radical of the triple shrinks
geometrically relative to `c` even though `c` itself explodes. Why now? Our single
witness `1 + 8 = 9` is the first member of exactly this tower, and the divisibility
engine behind it (the 2-adic valuation of `3^(2ⁿ) − 1`) is elementary enough to
formalise, turning one example into an infinite supply.

## 3. A radical-strong-multiplicativity criterion detects squarefree numbers

**Conjecture.** A positive integer `n` is squarefree if and only if
`rad(n) = n`, and more quantitatively the deficiency `n / rad(n)` equals the largest
square dividing `n` only when `n` is itself a perfect-square times a squarefree core;
the average size of `n / rad(n)` over `n ≤ X` converges to a constant.

The key insight is that `rad` collapses a number to its squarefree kernel, so the
ratio `n / rad(n)` is a clean measure of "powerfulness", and its averaged behaviour
encodes the density of squarefree numbers (`6/π²`). Why now? The equivalence
`rad n = n ↔ Squarefree n` is already established here, providing the exact hinge on
which the averaged statement turns.

## 4. ABC controls additive relations among smooth numbers

**Conjecture.** For every `ε > 0`, only finitely many coprime triples `a + b = c`
have all of `a, b, c` composed solely of primes below `(log c)^(1+ε)`.

The key insight is that smoothness caps the radical from above, so a smooth solution
would have an enormous quality, contradicting the boundedness that ABC predicts. Why
now? The conditional machinery here reduces such finiteness statements to a single
inequality between `c` and a power of `rad(abc)`, exactly the form ABC supplies.

## 5. The Fermat threshold is small and explicit

**Conjecture.** Under ABC with the explicit constant from the `ε = 1` regime, the
exponent threshold beyond which `xⁿ + yⁿ = zⁿ` is unsolvable can be taken below a
modest absolute number (single or low double digits), not merely "some large `N`".

The key insight is that the bound `zⁿ ≤ K·z⁶` already pins `n − 6` below `log₂ K`, so
any honest numerical value of `K` immediately yields a concrete, checkable threshold.
Why now? The proof produced here packages the constant transparently through the
`ε = 1` specialisation, so replacing the abstract `K` with a measured value is a
direct, finite refinement rather than a new idea.

import Mathlib

/-!
# Combinatorial Nerve: Euler characteristic of finite simplicial complexes

This file develops the numerical backbone of the *combinatorial nerve chain complex*.
A finite simplicial complex is modelled as a finite set of faces
`X : Finset (Finset V)`, each face being the finite set of its vertices.  Its Euler
characteristic is the signed face count `eulerChar X = ∑_{σ ∈ X} (-1)^{|σ|}`.

The combinatorial nerve construction covers `X` by subcomplexes `A₁, …, A_k`, forms
the intersections `Y_S = ⋂_{i ∈ S} A_i`, and assembles a bigraded chain complex out
of the critical cells of an acyclic gradient vector field on each `Y_S`.  Because that
construction is chain homotopy equivalent to the simplicial chain complex of `X`, all
of its homotopy invariants must agree with those of `X`.  The most accessible such
invariant is the Euler characteristic, and this file establishes the two structural
identities that make the Euler characteristic of the nerve complex computable:

* `CombinatorialNerve.eulerChar_biUnion` — the **nerve / inclusion–exclusion identity**:
  the Euler characteristic of a complex covered by `A` equals the alternating sum, over
  non-empty index subsets `S`, of the Euler characteristics of the intersections `Y_S`.
  This is the Mayer–Vietoris shadow of the nerve theorem at the level of `χ`.

* `CombinatorialNerve.eulerChar_eq_sum_by_dim` — the **dimension grouping identity**
  (equivalently, the discrete-Morse equality for the trivial gradient vector field, in
  which every face is critical): `χ` equals the alternating sum of the number of faces
  of each dimension.

These feed `Catalog/Cryptography/CombinatorialNerve/NerveComplex.lean`, where the
total-degree bookkeeping of the bigraded nerve complex is carried out.

## References (catalog)
* `nerve theorem`, `chain homotopy equivalence`, `discrete Morse theory`.
-/

namespace CombinatorialNerve

open Finset

variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {ι : Type*}

/-- Euler characteristic of a finite simplicial complex, presented as a finite set of
faces `X : Finset (Finset V)`: the signed count `∑_{σ ∈ X} (-1)^{|σ|}`.  (Using `(-1)^{|σ|}`
rather than `(-1)^{dim σ}` shifts the reduced Euler characteristic by an overall sign;
it remains an additive invariant, which is all the nerve bookkeeping needs.) -/
def eulerChar (X : Finset (Finset V)) : ℤ := ∑ σ ∈ X, (-1) ^ σ.card

/-- The intersection `Y_S = ⋂_{i ∈ S} A_i` of the cover pieces indexed by a finite set
`t`, as a finite set of faces.  For the empty index set we return `∅`; only non-empty `t`
ever occurs in the nerve construction. -/
def YS (A : ι → Finset (Finset V)) (t : Finset ι) : Finset (Finset V) :=
  if h : t.Nonempty then t.inf' h A else ∅

@[simp] lemma YS_of_nonempty (A : ι → Finset (Finset V)) {t : Finset ι} (h : t.Nonempty) :
    YS A t = t.inf' h A := by
  rw [YS, dif_pos h]

/-- **Nerve / inclusion–exclusion identity for the Euler characteristic.**

If a finite simplicial complex is the union `⋃_{i ∈ s} A_i` of the subcomplexes `A i`,
then its Euler characteristic is the alternating sum over all non-empty subsets
`t ⊆ s` of the Euler characteristics of the intersections `Y_t = ⋂_{i ∈ t} A_i`.

This is exactly the contribution the nerve makes: the index `t` is a simplex of the
nerve, of "nerve dimension" `|t| - 1`, contributing with sign `(-1)^{|t|+1}`. -/
theorem eulerChar_biUnion (s : Finset ι) (A : ι → Finset (Finset V)) :
    eulerChar (s.biUnion A) =
      ∑ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty), (-1) ^ (t.card + 1) * eulerChar (YS A t) := by
  unfold eulerChar
  rw [Finset.inclusion_exclusion_sum_biUnion,
    ← Finset.sum_coe_sort (s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty))]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro t _
  rw [zsmul_eq_mul,
    show YS A t.1 = t.1.inf' (mem_filter.1 t.2).2 A from by rw [YS, dif_pos]]
  push_cast
  ring

omit [DecidableEq V] in
/-- **Dimension grouping identity** (the discrete-Morse equality for the trivial
gradient vector field, in which every face is critical).

The Euler characteristic equals the alternating sum, over the realised dimensions
`d = |σ|`, of the number of faces of that dimension.  This is the `E¹`-page input on
each cover piece: it expresses `χ(Y_S)` as a signed count of critical cells. -/
theorem eulerChar_eq_sum_by_dim (X : Finset (Finset V)) :
    eulerChar X =
      ∑ d ∈ X.image (·.card), (-1) ^ d * ((X.filter (fun σ => σ.card = d)).card : ℤ) := by
  unfold eulerChar
  rw [← Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to (g := fun σ => σ.card) (t := X.image (·.card))
        (fun σ hσ => Finset.mem_image_of_mem _ hσ)]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro d _
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl (g := fun _ => (-1 : ℤ) ^ d)
        (by intro σ hσ; rw [(mem_filter.1 hσ).2]),
      Finset.sum_const, nsmul_eq_mul, mul_comm]

# The bigraded combinatorial nerve chain complex and its Euler characteristic

The combinatorial nerve chain complex `C_*(X; V)` of a finite simplicial complex `X`
covered by subcomplexes `A₁, …, A_k` is *bigraded*: a generator in total degree `n` is a
pair `(S, σ)` where `S ⊆ [k]` is a non-empty index set (a simplex of the nerve, of nerve
dimension `|S| - 1`) and `σ` is an `m`-dimensional critical simplex of an acyclic gradient
vector field `V_S` on the intersection `Y_S`, subject to `n = m + (|S| - 1)`.  Equivalently
`C_n(X; V) = ⨁_{S} ⟨critical (n - |S| + 1)-simplices of V_S⟩`.

The differential mixes the internal discrete-Morse differential of each `V_S` with the
nerve face maps defined through gradient trajectories between intersections.  The headline
theorem of the topic is that `C_*(X; V)` is **chain homotopy equivalent** to the simplicial
chain complex of `X`.

This file formalises the Euler-characteristic content of that equivalence — the strongest
numerical invariant it implies — purely combinatorially:

* `CombinatorialNerve.nerveTotalEuler` — the Euler characteristic of the total complex,
  the signed count of bigraded generators `(S, m)` with the total-degree sign
  `(-1)^{m + |S| - 1}`.
* `CombinatorialNerve.nerveRank` — the rank of the chain group `C_n(X; V)`, i.e. the number
  of bigraded generators in total degree `n`.
* `CombinatorialNerve.nerveTotalEuler_eq_signed` — the **`E¹`-page sign factorisation**:
  the total-degree sign splits as the product of the nerve sign `(-1)^{|S|+1}` and the
  internal Morse sign `(-1)^m`.  This is the spectral-sequence sign convention made precise.
* `CombinatorialNerve.nerve_degree_grading` — the **total-complex identity**: grouping the
  bigraded generators by total degree `n` and taking the alternating sum of ranks recovers
  the total Euler characteristic.
* `CombinatorialNerve.nerveTotalEuler_eq_eulerChar` and the capstone
  `CombinatorialNerve.eulerChar_eq_degreeGraded_nerve` — assuming the per-piece discrete
  Morse equality (`χ(Y_S)` = signed critical-cell count, the defining property of an acyclic
  gradient vector field), the alternating sum of the ranks of the nerve chain groups equals
  `χ(X)`.  This is exactly the Euler-characteristic shadow of the chain homotopy equivalence.

## References (catalog)
* `discrete Morse theory`, `nerve theorem`, `spectral sequence`,
  `chain homotopy equivalence`, `gradient trajectories`.
-/

namespace CombinatorialNerve

open Finset

variable {V : Type*} [DecidableEq V] {ι : Type*}

/-- Euler characteristic of the total combinatorial nerve complex: the signed count of
bigraded generators `(t, m)` (with `t` a non-empty index set and `m < D` a critical
dimension), where `c t m` is the number of `m`-dimensional critical simplices of the
acyclic gradient vector field on `Y_t`, and the total-degree sign is `(-1)^{m + |t| - 1}`. -/
def nerveTotalEuler (s : Finset ι) (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  ∑ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty), ∑ m ∈ range D, (-1) ^ (m + t.card - 1) * c t m

/-- Rank of the chain group `C_n(X; V)`: the number of bigraded generators `(t, m)` whose
total degree `m + |t| - 1` equals `n`. -/
def nerveRank (s : Finset ι) (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D : ℕ) (n : ℕ) : ℤ :=
  ∑ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty), ∑ m ∈ range D,
    if m + t.card - 1 = n then c t m else 0

/-- **`E¹`-page sign factorisation.**  The total-degree sign `(-1)^{m + |t| - 1}` of a
bigraded generator factors as the nerve sign `(-1)^{|t|+1}` times the internal discrete-Morse
sign `(-1)^m`.  Consequently the total Euler characteristic is the alternating sum over the
nerve of the per-piece Morse Euler characteristics — the first page of the Mayer–Vietoris /
nerve spectral sequence. -/
theorem nerveTotalEuler_eq_signed (s : Finset ι) (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D : ℕ) :
    nerveTotalEuler s c D =
      ∑ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty),
        (-1) ^ (t.card + 1) * ∑ m ∈ range D, (-1) ^ m * c t m := by
  unfold nerveTotalEuler
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro t ht
  rw [mem_filter] at ht
  have hs : 1 ≤ t.card := Finset.card_pos.mpr ht.2
  rw [Finset.mul_sum]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro m _
  have key : ((-1 : ℤ)) ^ (m + t.card - 1) = (-1) ^ (t.card + 1) * (-1) ^ m := by
    have e : m + t.card - 1 + 2 = (t.card + 1) + m := by omega
    have h2 : ((-1 : ℤ)) ^ (m + t.card - 1) * (-1) ^ 2 = (-1) ^ (t.card + 1) * (-1) ^ m := by
      rw [← pow_add, ← pow_add, e]
    simpa using h2
  rw [key]; ring

/-- **Total-complex identity.**  Grouping the bigraded generators by total degree `n` and
taking the alternating sum of the ranks `C_n(X; V)` reproduces the Euler characteristic of
the total complex.  Here `B` is any degree bound exceeding every realised total degree. -/
theorem nerve_degree_grading (s : Finset ι) (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D B : ℕ)
    (hB : ∀ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty), ∀ m ∈ range D, m + t.card - 1 < B) :
    (∑ n ∈ range B, (-1) ^ n * nerveRank s c D n) = nerveTotalEuler s c D := by
  unfold nerveRank nerveTotalEuler
  simp_rw [Finset.mul_sum]
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro t ht
  rw [Finset.sum_comm]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro m hm
  have hlt := hB t ht m hm
  rw [Finset.sum_congr rfl
        (g := fun x => if m + t.card - 1 = x then (-1) ^ (m + t.card - 1) * c t m else 0)
        (by intro x _; split_ifs with h <;> simp [h]),
      Finset.sum_ite_eq (range B) (m + t.card - 1) (fun _ => (-1) ^ (m + t.card - 1) * c t m),
      if_pos (mem_range.mpr hlt)]

/-- **Euler characteristic of the nerve complex equals `χ(X)`.**

Assume `X = ⋃_{i ∈ s} A_i` and that on each non-empty intersection `Y_t` the acyclic
gradient vector field satisfies the discrete Morse equality `χ(Y_t) = ∑_m (-1)^m · c t m`
(the signed count of its critical cells).  Then the Euler characteristic of the total
combinatorial nerve complex equals `χ(X)`.

This is the Euler-characteristic consequence of the chain homotopy equivalence
`C_*(X; V) ≃ C_*^{simp}(X)`, proved here from inclusion–exclusion over the nerve. -/
theorem nerveTotalEuler_eq_eulerChar (s : Finset ι) (A : ι → Finset (Finset V))
    (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D : ℕ)
    (hMorse : ∀ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty),
      eulerChar (YS A t) = ∑ m ∈ range D, (-1) ^ m * c t m) :
    nerveTotalEuler s c D = eulerChar (s.biUnion A) := by
  rw [nerveTotalEuler_eq_signed, eulerChar_biUnion]
  apply Finset.sum_congr rfl
  intro t ht
  rw [hMorse t ht]

/-- **Capstone: the combinatorial nerve chain complex computes `χ(X)`.**

The alternating sum of the ranks of the nerve chain groups `C_n(X; V)`, grouped by total
degree `n < B`, equals the Euler characteristic of `X`.  This is the full numerical
statement implied by `C_*(X; V) ≃ C_*^{simp}(X)`: it combines the total-complex degree
grading with inclusion–exclusion over the nerve and the per-piece discrete Morse equality. -/
theorem eulerChar_eq_degreeGraded_nerve (s : Finset ι) (A : ι → Finset (Finset V))
    (c : Finset ι → ℕ → ℤ) (D B : ℕ)
    (hB : ∀ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty), ∀ m ∈ range D, m + t.card - 1 < B)
    (hMorse : ∀ t ∈ s.powerset.filter (·.Nonempty),
      eulerChar (YS A t) = ∑ m ∈ range D, (-1) ^ m * c t m) :
    (∑ n ∈ range B, (-1) ^ n * nerveRank s c D n) = eulerChar (s.biUnion A) := by
  rw [nerve_degree_grading s c D B hB, nerveTotalEuler_eq_eulerChar s A c D hMorse]

# Computational Evidence — Combinatorial Nerve Euler Characteristic

We model a finite simplicial complex as a finite set of faces `X ⊆ 𝒫(V)` (each face is
the finite set of its vertices), with Euler characteristic the signed face count

    χ(X) = ∑_{σ ∈ X} (-1)^{|σ|}.

(Using `(-1)^{|σ|}` rather than `(-1)^{dim σ} = (-1)^{|σ|-1}` flips the overall sign of the
reduced Euler characteristic; it keeps every exponent a genuine natural number and remains an
additive set invariant, which is all the nerve bookkeeping requires.)

## 1. Small-case calculations

### 1a. A combinatorial circle ∂Δ²
Vertices `{0},{1},{2}`; edges `{0,1},{1,2},{0,2}`.

    χ = 3·(-1)^1 + 3·(-1)^2 = -3 + 3 = 0.

This matches the (sign-shifted) Euler characteristic of `S¹`. Verified in Lean as
`example : eulerChar circle = 0 := by decide`.

### 1b. Inclusion–exclusion over a 2-set cover (Mayer–Vietoris check)
Cover the circle by two arcs:

    A₀ = {0},{1},{2},{0,1},{0,2}     (everything except edge {1,2})
    A₁ = {0},{1},{2},{1,2}           (the remaining edge and its vertices)

Then `A₀ ∪ A₁ = circle`, and the intersection is `Y_{0,1} = {0},{1},{2}` (three vertices).

    χ(A₀) = 3·(-1) + 2·(+1) = -1
    χ(A₁) = 3·(-1) + 1·(+1) = -2
    χ(Y_{0,1}) = 3·(-1) = -3

Nerve / inclusion–exclusion alternating sum (signs `(-1)^{|t|+1}`):

    χ(A₀) + χ(A₁) - χ(Y_{0,1}) = (-1) + (-2) - (-3) = 0 = χ(circle).  ✓

This is exactly `eulerChar_biUnion`.

### 1c. Bigraded sign factorisation (E¹ page)
A bigraded generator `(t, m)` (nerve index `t`, internal Morse dimension `m`) sits in total
degree `n = m + |t| - 1` and carries sign `(-1)^{m + |t| - 1}`. Checking the factorisation
`(-1)^{m+|t|-1} = (-1)^{|t|+1}·(-1)^m`:

    |t|=1: (-1)^{m}      = (-1)^2·(-1)^m = (-1)^m            ✓
    |t|=2: (-1)^{m+1}    = (-1)^3·(-1)^m = -(-1)^m           ✓
    |t|=3: (-1)^{m+2}    = (-1)^4·(-1)^m = (-1)^m            ✓

So the nerve sign and the internal Morse sign separate cleanly. This is
`nerveTotalEuler_eq_signed`.

### 1d. Degree grading collapses to χ(X)
Take the trivial all-critical gradient field on each `Y_t` (every face critical), so
`c t m = #{m-dimensional faces of Y_t}` and the per-piece discrete Morse equality
`χ(Y_t) = ∑_m (-1)^m c t m` holds by definition (this is `eulerChar_eq_sum_by_dim`).
With the 2-arc cover of 1b and `D = 2`, `B = 3`:

    nerveRank n = (#bigraded generators in total degree n)
    ∑_n (-1)^n · nerveRank n = 0 = χ(circle).  ✓

This is the capstone `eulerChar_eq_degreeGraded_nerve`.

## 2. OEIS / sequence note

The alternating binomial structure of the nerve signs over a `k`-element cover is governed by
`∑_{j=1}^{k} (-1)^{j+1} C(k,j) = 1` (the nonempty-subset alternating sum), i.e. the first
difference of the all-ones sequence; the row sums of signed Pascal data
(OEIS A000007 / A130595-type alternating identities). No new sequence is introduced; the
content is the *bigraded* coupling of these nerve signs with the internal Morse signs.

## 3. Counterexample hunt

- **Drop the nerve signs** `(-1)^{|t|+1}` in `eulerChar_biUnion`: fails already on 1b

No counterexample to the stated (guarded) theorems was found; each guard corresponds to a
genuine boundary of validity.

All four computational checks agree with the formal theorems in
`EulerCharacteristic.lean` and `NerveComplex.lean`. The evidence supports the claim that the
ranks of the combinatorial nerve chain groups reproduce `χ(X)` — the Euler-characteristic
shadow of the chain homotopy equivalence — and pins down precisely which sign data and bounds
are required.

# Future Directions — Combinatorial Nerve Chain Homotopy Equivalence

This cycle isolated, at the level of the Euler characteristic, the precise sign and
boundedness data that make the combinatorial nerve chain complex of a covered finite
simplicial complex agree with the complex itself: a multiplicative split of the total-degree
sign into a *nerve* part and an *internal Morse* part, an inclusion–exclusion identity over
the nerve, and a bounded-strip degree grading. The following conjectures push from this
numerical shadow toward the full homotopical statement and its applications.

## Conjecture 1 — Functorial sign-coherent nerve differential

For any finite cover of a finite simplicial complex by subcomplexes, equipped with an acyclic
discrete gradient field on every intersection, the bigraded generators assemble into a chain
complex whose differential is the sum of the internal Morse differential and a nerve face map
defined by counting gradient trajectories between adjacent intersections, with the two pieces
sign-coordinated by the factorisation `sign(total) = sign(nerve)·sign(Morse)`. This complex is
chain homotopy equivalent to the simplicial chain complex of the whole space, *uniformly in
the choice of gradient fields*.

The key insight is that the total-degree sign factors exactly into a nerve parity and a Morse
parity, so the two differentials anticommute by construction and no choice-dependent
correction terms are needed to make `d² = 0`.

Why now? The Euler-characteristic identity already forces the two sign systems to be
compatible on every bigraded line; the only remaining obstruction to lifting the equality of
invariants to an equivalence of complexes is the trajectory-counting face map, which recent
advances in algorithmic discrete Morse theory make explicitly computable.

## Conjecture 2 — Collapsibility certificate for distributed verification

If every pairwise (and higher) intersection in a cover admits a gradient field with a single
critical cell, then the entire complex is homotopy equivalent to the nerve, and a short,
locally-checkable certificate (one collapsing sequence per intersection plus the nerve's face
data) suffices to verify the global homotopy type. The certificate size is linear in the total
number of critical cells, independent of the size of the ambient complex.

The key insight is that contractible intersections collapse the bigraded complex onto its
nerve row, so global topological information is recoverable from strictly local, independently
auditable data.

Why now? Distributed and zero-knowledge settings increasingly demand global structural
guarantees assembled from local, separately attestable pieces; a nerve-based certificate turns
a topological assertion about a large shared structure into a bundle of small local proofs.

## Conjecture 3 — Strong Morse inequalities for the nerve complex

The ranks of the combinatorial nerve chain groups satisfy the full strong Morse inequalities
against the Betti numbers of the covered space: the alternating partial sums of nerve ranks
dominate the corresponding alternating partial sums of Betti numbers, with equality in the top
degree. Consequently the minimal achievable total nerve rank over all admissible gradient
fields equals the total Betti number of the space.

The key insight is that the degree grading already collapses the bigraded ranks to the correct
Euler characteristic under a single boundedness hypothesis; promoting the alternating sum to
the alternating *partial* sums upgrades the equality to the sharp chain of inequalities.

Why now? Optimal (minimal-critical-cell) gradient fields are now reachable in practice, making
the bound on minimal nerve rank an operational target rather than a purely existential one.

## Conjecture 4 — Nerve spectral sequence degeneration criterion

The Mayer–Vietoris spectral sequence whose first page is the bigraded nerve complex degenerates
at the second page precisely when every nonempty intersection is acyclic in all but one degree.
Under this condition the homology of the covered space is computed directly by the homology of
the nerve with coefficients in the locally constant system of intersection homologies.

The key insight is that the clean multiplicative separation of nerve and Morse signs makes the
first differential of the spectral sequence purely combinatorial, so degeneration is controlled
entirely by the acyclicity profile of the intersections rather than by the embedding geometry.

Why now? Cover-based computation of homology scales far better than global methods on large
complexes; a sharp, checkable degeneration criterion tells a practitioner exactly when the
cheap nerve computation is provably exact.

## Conjecture 5 — Stability of the nerve invariant under cover refinement

Refining a cover (subdividing a piece, or adding an overlapping piece) changes the bigraded
nerve complex only up to chain homotopy: the resulting Euler characteristic, and more strongly
the homotopy type of the total complex, are invariant. The refinement induces an explicit
chain homotopy whose size is controlled by the number of new intersections created.

The key insight is that inclusion–exclusion over the nerve is already invariant under refining
the index set, so the numerical invariant cannot move; the bounded correction term measures the
homotopical, not numerical, cost of refinement.

Why now? Adaptive multi-resolution covers are standard in large-scale geometric data analysis,
and a quantitative refinement-stability statement underwrites incremental, streaming
computation of topological summaries.

rationale.novelty: The two main theorems are well-known combinatorial identities, not new mathematical results. (1) `eulerChar_biUnion` is the inclusion-exclusion principle applied to the additive functional σ ↦ (-1)^|σ| — a classical result that follows directly from Mathlib's `Finset.inclusion_exclusion_sum_biUnion`. (2) `eulerChar_eq_sum_by_dim` is a trivial fiberwise regrouping of the defining sum of Euler characteristic by face cardinality — essentially just reindexing a summation. The conceptual packaging connecting these to the nerve theorem and discrete Morse theory is interesting, but the actual mathematical content formalized is standard. Neither theorem represents a genuinely new connection; they are routine consequences of known combinatorial identities applied to a standard topological invariant. The only marginal novelty is the Lean formalization itself and the sign convention choices, which is engineering rather than mathematical novelty.
rationale.depth: While the surrounding documentation describes a deep topological concept (Combinatorial Nerve Chain Homotopy Equivalence), the actual formalized theorems are elementary numerical shadows of this concept: an inclusion-exclusion formula for Euler characteristic and a dimension-grouping identity. The proofs rely heavily on existing general library lemmas (Finset.inclusion_exclusion_sum_biUnion and Finset.sum_fiberwise_of_maps_to) and consist mostly of definitional unfolding, type conversions (zsmul_eq_mul, push_cast), and basic algebraic rearrangement (ring). There are no novel definitions or deep mathematical insights in the proof scripts themselves; they are standard combinatorial identities achieved via library plumbing.
